key_findings: Execution strategies in Python workflow engines follow clear patterns: ExecutionResult-based control flow (proceed/sleep/hold), state persistence, and dependency resolution
Strategy pattern decouples algorithmic implementation from orchestration logic—orchestration should not know algorithm details to avoid becoming a 'god function'
Modern workflow engines use DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) based task chaining with inter-task data passing (XCom pattern in Airflow, equivalent patterns in Prefect/Dagster)
Customizable processor/middleware patterns enable different execution strategies: exception handling, resource processing, and conditional branching
Durable execution patterns (Temporal, Dapr Workflows) persist workflow state to enable recovery and horizontal scaling across distributed systems
Pure Python implementations (SpiffWorkflow, liteflow) avoid external dependencies while supporting BPMN/DMN standards for low-code visualization
Distributed execution frameworks (Ray, Dask) integrated with modern engines (Prefect, Flyte) enable efficient parallel execution strategies at scale
best_practices: Decouple orchestration from execution logic using the strategy pattern—orchestration file should not contain algorithm details
Use ExecutionResult objects to control workflow flow (proceed with outcome, sleep, or hold state)
Implement persistence layer for workflow context and state to enable recovery and resumption
Chain tasks via DAG with explicit dependency resolution rather than linear sequential execution
Use inter-task data passing (XCom pattern) to avoid tight coupling between task implementations
Support pluggable middleware/processor pattern to customize behavior (exception handling, logging, validation)
Choose engine based on use case: YAML-based (Kestra) for ETL, code-based (Temporal) for mission-critical reliability, Python-native (Prefect) for ML/data science
warnings: Orchestration files become 'god functions' if they couple to algorithmic implementation details—changes in implementation will cause orchestration failures
Custom engines without external dependencies still require dependency resolution logic to avoid deadlocks in complex workflows
Silent fallback in distributed execution can mask failures—explicit error boundaries and retry strategies are essential
Mixing persistence strategies (in-memory vs. persistent storage) without clear semantics leads to hard-to-debug state inconsistencies
recommended_tools: Temporal — for durable, mission-critical workflows with recovery guarantees
Prefect — Python-native with Ray/Dask integration for distributed execution in ML/data workflows
Dapr Workflows — durable workflow-as-code at scale across Python, JS, .NET, Java, Go
SpiffWorkflow — pure Python with BPMN/DMN support for low-code business applications
Airflow (Apache) — established DAG-based ETL with XCom inter-task data passing
Kestra — YAML-based workflow orchestration optimized for ETL and data pipelines
Flyte — type-safe Python workflows with distributed execution capabilities

strategic_insights.execution_profile_pattern: Workflows track execution state through ExecutionResult objects that signal next action (proceed, sleep, hold). This separates control flow from task logic.
strategic_insights.strategy_pattern_role: Encapsulates different execution strategies (sequential, parallel, conditional, retry) so orchestration doesn't couple to specific implementations. Critical for reusability.
strategic_insights.state_persistence: Persistent context enables resumption from failures and horizontal scaling. Pure Python engines use in-memory state; durable engines (Temporal, Dapr) persist to external stores.
strategic_insights.distributed_execution: Modern engines integrate Ray/Dask for parallel task execution. Strategy pattern allows swapping local vs. distributed execution without changing orchestration code.
